content: The scope of antenatal care services includes monitoring programmatic targets, particularly in countries with policies for targeted hepatitis B virus (HBV) vaccination at birth. This involves tracking the number of individuals tested for hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) during a reporting period. Specifically, this includes individuals attending HIV prevention services, people living with HIV, and pregnant women. The denominator is the total number of individuals attending HIV treatment or prevention services during the same period, categorized similarly. These tools are essential for tracking hepatitis and HIV testing services at both facility and community levels. The percentage of individuals tested for hepatitis C virus (HCV) during a reporting period is also monitored. This includes those attending HIV prevention services and people living with HIV. Testing for HCV co-infection among people living with HIV helps clinicians determine the need for further evaluation and treatment adjustments. Disaggregated data can identify gaps in diagnosing HCV infections. The percentage of individuals with a positive HBsAg test result during the reporting period is another critical indicator. This includes individuals attending HIV prevention services, people living with HIV, and pregnant women. Testing for HBV identifies co-infections with HIV, enabling adjustments to HIV treatment regimens to address chronic HBV infection. The HBsAg positivity rate among antenatal care attendees can also provide insights into the HBV burden in the population. Tenofovir, combined with lamivudine or emtricitabine, is the preferred treatment for individuals co-infected with HIV and HBV. This regimen is also suitable for individuals with tuberculosis and pregnant women. The percentage of people living with HIV and diagnosed with HCV infection who initiated HCV treatment during the reporting period is tracked. Treating HCV among people living with HIV improves quality of life, life expectancy, and reduces mortality. The percentage of people living with HIV and co-infected with HCV who were confirmed cured of HCV during the reporting period is another key indicator. Sustained virological response (SVR) is assessed 12–24 weeks after treatment completion to confirm cure. The number of women screened using any test (e.g., HPV DNA test, visual inspection with acetic acid, cytology) is recorded. Screening intervals depend on the test used, and each individual is counted only once during the reporting period. The percentage of women living with HIV who screened positive for pre-invasive cervical disease and received treatment is tracked to assess treatment coverage. Treatment options include thermal ablation, cryotherapy, and excision procedures. This indicator aligns with the WHO Global Strategy to eliminate cervical cancer by vaccinating 90% of eligible girls against HPV, screening 70% of eligible women at least twice in their lifetime, and treating 90% of those with positive screening results or cervical lesions by 2030. Over time, the number of women receiving treatment is expected to plateau and decrease as screening programs expand and HPV vaccination coverage increases. This indicator tracks the percentage of women living with HIV who are still alive 12 months after their diagnosis. In settings with good retention and follow-up, five-year survival rates can also be calculated. HIV incidence is estimated as the number of people newly infected with HIV per 1,000 uninfected individuals. Mathematical modeling tools, such as Spectrum AIM, incorporate data from surveys, surveillance, and programmatic records to estimate HIV incidence. This indicator assesses the impact of HIV prevention, care, and treatment programs. Effective diagnosis and treatment under the Treat All approach should significantly reduce AIDS-related deaths. This includes avoiding general health care, HIV testing, HIV medical care, or HIV treatment due to fear of stigma, violence, harassment, or arrest. Tracking this indicator helps identify areas where efforts to reduce discrimination and improve service utilization should be focused. This indicator provides insights into the extent of perceived stigma in health care settings and helps guide efforts to reduce discrimination and improve access to care.
